stem: The physiological value of food is the actual energy produced by 1 g of it. These values are 4.0 Kcal/g for carbohydrate, 4.0 Kcal/g for protein and 9.0 Kcal/g for fat. A meal supplies 20 g of carbohydrate, 10 g of protein and 5 g of fat. What is the total energy actually produced by this meal?

distractor_rationale.A: The gross calorific value 4.1 Kcal/g has been used for the carbohydrate instead of its physiological value 4.0 Kcal/g.
distractor_rationale.B: The gross calorific value 5.65 Kcal/g has been used for the protein although the question asks for the energy actually produced.
distractor_rationale.D: The gross calorific values 4.1, 5.65 and 9.45 Kcal/g have been used throughout, which gives the heat of combustion and not the energy actually produced.

formula_principle: Energy produced equals the sum over each food type of mass in grams multiplied by the physiological value in Kcal per gram.
common_misconception: Students use the gross calorific value, which is the heat liberated on complete combustion of 1 g of food in a bomb calorimeter, when the energy actually produced by the body is asked for.

distractor_rationale.B: The difference of 0.45 Kcal/g for the 10 g of fat has been left out of the total.
distractor_rationale.C: The difference of 0.1 Kcal/g for the 50 g of carbohydrate has been dismissed as negligible and omitted.

formula_principle: The excess equals the sum over each food type of mass in grams multiplied by the difference between its gross calorific value and its physiological value per gram.
common_misconception: Students treat gross calorific value and physiological value as the same quantity for carbohydrate and fat because the two figures are close, and count only the protein gap.
